title: Database Relationships
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of database relationships in a FastAPI application.
Apply or interpret one example related to one-to-one relationships.
Identify one limitation or failure case and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson covers database relationships within database integration. Use the supplied syllabus topics as the coverage checklist, then connect them to the worked example and the verification task.
content.why_it_matters: You will use database relationships to build APIs whose contracts and behavior are understandable to both clients and maintainers. The practical aim is data integrity, transaction boundaries, schema evolution and bounded database access.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Database Relationships matters because it is part of database integration. In practice, focus on data integrity, transaction boundaries, schema evolution and bounded database access. A framework feature only helps when its assumptions match the application; keep input validation, business policy and side effects distinguishable.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Database Relationships
content_blocks.code:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text

engine = create_engine("sqlite:///./lab.db")
with engine.begin() as connection:
    result = connection.execute(text("SELECT 1 AS ok"))
    print(result.scalar_one())
content_blocks.run_instructions: This tiny SQLAlchemy connection smoke test uses local SQLite. Use parameterized statements for values; place real credentials in environment configuration.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For read-only examples, no reset is needed. For any example that writes state, use a disposable local database/test fixture; record the starting state and clean up only lab data. Never use production credentials or real personal data.
content_blocks.limitations: This code is inspectable lesson material, not executed by CodeLeaf. Run it only in a local virtual environment or a separately isolated runner with resource/time/network limits. Security examples are sketches, not complete production authentication or authorization systems.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Adapt the example to cover “One-to-one relationships”. Write down the expected success result and one invalid, missing, duplicate, timeout or permission-boundary case that matters for this topic.

expected_output: A reviewable example or design note for Database Relationships, covering the PDF subtopics, expected behavior and at least one verification check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a code fragment without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Installed versions, imported types, application structure and external services affect behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: State assumptions; check the versioned official docs; run a minimal local test and add one failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one happy-path response as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Invalid input, permissions, concurrency, timeouts and cleanup are not exercised by a single request.
common_mistakes.fix: Add focused normal and negative tests and record exact expected status/body.

common_mistakes.why: Even short examples may mutate records, reveal data or affect availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic inputs and a disposable environment; review security, cleanup and rollback before promotion.
